files.title: File:Banner of the messengers of Genghis Khan to Nishapur (1423 painting, color). Supplément Persan 1443.jpg
files.description: Banner of the messengers of Genghis Khan to Nishapur (1423 painting, color). Supplément Persan 1443 "The earliest-known representation [of the sun and lion] as a banner device ( Figure 18 ) is from a miniature painting illustrating a copy, dated 826/1423, of the Šāh-nāma of Šams-al-Dīn Kāšānī—an epic composition on the Mongol conquest (Bibliothèque Nationale, suppl. no. 1443). It shows several (Mongol?) horsemen approaching a walled city (Nīšāpūr), and one of them carries a tall banner which is crowned by a spear-head within a crescent moon (the māhča-ye lewāʾ) and its square background bears a lion passant with a rising sun on its back and two floating pennons (Blochet, 1928, III, p. 180). A similar early depiction ( Figure 19 ) is on a large, double-paged miniature dated ca. 865/1460 ( Martin, Pls. 60 f. )." Encyclopedia Iranica
files.credit: This image has been extracted from another file

files.title: File:Birth of Muhammad from folio 44a of the Jami‘ al-tawarikh.jpg
files.description: Birth of Prophet Muhammad. Picture from folio 44a of the Jami‘ al-tawarikh, Iran (Tabriz), c. A.H. 714/A.D. 1314–15 The manuscript is located at Edinburgh University Library (MS Arab 20, folio 42r),Cat. 6. The illustrators of the Jami often borrowed iconography from other traditions, such as Christian manuscripts, to create their images. For the birth of Muhammad, they adapted a Christian nativity scene. The three women on the left take the place of the three magi. The grandfather of the prophet Abd al-Muttalib on the right takes the place of Joseph. In other images, the compositions might be original, but stock figures would be used in them.
files.credit: Blair, Sheila; Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, Rashīd al-Dīn Ṭabīb (1995) A compendium of chronicles: Rashid al-Din's illustrated history of the world , Nour Foundation in association with Azimuth Editions and Oxford University Press, pp. 68−69 ISBN : 9780197276273 .

files.title: File:Bataille de vâliyân (1221).jpeg
files.description: Battle of Vâliyân (1221). Jami' al-tawarikh , Rashid al-Din . "Mongol officers Taqacaq and Mulgar attempted to take Waliyan. Jalal al-Din moved to Parwan; making a quick move across the mountains to the north, he surprised and routed the Mongols at Waliyan, inflincting a reported 1,000 loss on them. The Mongols retreated across a river and destroyed a bridge to keep the enemy from following (spring 1221). Jalal al-Din had left his baggage at Parwan and returned there." [1]
files.credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France. Département des Manuscrits. Division orientale. Supplément persan 1113, fol. 72v

files.title: File:Council of Tuman, Köl Erki, Kayı Yavgu Han and Korkut, 1426-30 Herat, folio 387a. Jami al-Tawarikh, TSMK, H.1653.jpg
files.description: Council of Tuman, Köl Erki, Kayı Yavgu Khan and Korkut, 1426-30 Herat, folio 387a. Jami al-Tawarikh, TSMK, H.1653 "According to Reşideddin, Dede Korkut lived in the period after Oğuz Kagan. According to the information in the work, upon the will of Oğuz Kagan, Gün Khan succeeded his father. After Gün Khan, Dip Yabgu succeeded him. He also preserved the order established by his grandfather Oğuz Kagan. After Gün Khan, his other son Kurs Yabgu succeeded him. Then, Kuru Yasak Yabgu, İnal Yabgu, İnalsır Yasak Yabgu, Ala Atlı Kış Donlu Kayı İnal Khan, Tuman Khan , Diken Bile Er Biçken Kayı Yabgu Khan ascended to the throne in order. According to the work, Korkut lived in the time of Ala Atlı Kış Donlu Kayı İnal Khan, Köl Erki Khan , Tuman Khan , Diken Bile Er Biçken Kayı Yabgu Khan . Korkut here is Dede Korkut." p.12 "Beginning with Reshid ud-din, in the early fourteenth century, historians of the Oghuz described Korkut as a competent statesman and diplomat who served several of the ninth- and tenth-century kings who made Yeni Kent their capital: Inal Sir Yabgu , Kayi Inal Khan , and Tuman (whom he also named)." The Book of Dede Korkut: A Turkish Epic "There is no need to go deeply into the question of whether Dede Korkut was a real person; certainly there is no evidence that he was not. The historian Rashid al-Din (d. 1318) says that he lived for 295 years; that he appeared in the time of the Oghuz ruler Inal Syr Yavkuy Khan, by whom he was sent on an embassy to the Prophet; that he became a Muslim; that he gave advice to the Great Khan of the Oghuz, attended the election of the Great Khan, and gave names to children." in The book of Dede Korkut by Lewis, Geoffrey, p.12
files.credit: Two Copies of Câmi‘ü't-Tevârîh (H.1653-H.1654) in Topkapı Palace Manuscript Treasury, Zeren Tanındı, Filiz Çağman

files.title: File:DiezAlbumsComplainingWoman.jpg
files.description: A woman complaining to the ruler. Illustration of Rashid-ad-Din's Gami' at-tawarih. Tabriz (?), 1st quarter of 14th century. Water colours on paper. Original size: 11.8 cm x 25.8 cm. Staatsbibliothek Berlin, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 70, p. 18 no.2. This illustrates a story about Ghazan Khan. Because Ghazan had officials and military stay in the houses of the general population, an old man told Ghazan a story about a Sultan: near Nishapur, this sultan met a newlywed woman that led a horse to drink. This task had actually been given to her husband by a Turk soldier, who wanted the husband out of the house. The Sultan consequently had separate baracks built for his men. And so did Ghazan.
files.credit: Dschingis Khan und seine Erben (exhibition catalogue), München 2005, p. 273

Original size: 20.3 cm x 26.7 cm. Staatsbibliothek Berlin, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 70, p. 8 no.1. This seems to be a tent mosque. The inscription above the arch on the left, which is either the entrance or the Mihrab, reads "Allah is the ruler" (or similar). Note: the proportions given in the source seem rather inconsistent with those of the image.
files.credit: Dschingis Khan und seine Erben (exhibition catalogue), München 2005, p. 266

files.title: File:DiezAlbumsGhazanMausoleum.jpg
files.description: Ghazan Khan's mausoleum and foundation. Illustration of Rashid-ad-Din's Gami' at-tawarih. Tabriz (?), 1st quarter of 14th century. Water colours (and silver?) on paper. Original size: 36.2 cm x 29 cm. Staatsbibliothek Berlin, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 70, p. 13. "Two turbaned figured are in discussion at the gateway to a religious complex, which Karin Rührdanz plausibly identifies as Ghazan Khan's mausoleum in Tabriz . Note 78 (Diez A fol. 70, p.13)" The Diez Albums: Contexts and Contents pp.240-241 "Sktech of Ghazaniyeh , in Jami al-Tawarikh, written by Rashid al-Din" p.40 fig.6 left Recognizing the Architectural Form of “Ghazan’s Tomb” in “Abvab-Albar” collection of “Ghazaniyeh” and its Role in Iranian Urbanization Development, 2016, Bagh-e Nazar, University of Tehran
files.credit: Dschingis Khan und seine Erben (exhibition catalogue), München 2005, p. 267

files.title: File:Fall Of Baghdad (Diez Albums).jpg
files.description: Fall Of Baghdad (Diez Albums). Detail: a leading official's failed attempt to escape by boat from the city (center right): "The davāt-dār (chief secretary) who commanded the Caliph’s army was encamped between Baʿqūbā and Bājisrā. Hearing that the Mongol army was approaching from the west, the davāt-dār crossed the Tigris and joined battle with the Mongols near Anbār. The Mongols retreated and, joining Baiju ’s main army, opened a canal on the river Tigris. Half of the Caliph’s army was drowned and half was defeated in the attacks that followed. The davāt-dār made an attempt to escape by boat down the Tigris. Being unsuccessful, he fled back to Baghdad." in (2011) The Mongols and the Armenians (1220-1335) , Leiden ; Boston: Brill, p. 130 ISBN : 978-90-04-18635-4 .

files.title: File:Folio 21 verso. The pavilion called Frashi, built by order of Uktay Qa'an in the city of Qaraqorum with gold and silver statues made so as wine and qumiz, deposited in them, should run out of their mouths.jpg
files.description: Folio 2I verso. The pavilion called Frashi, built by order of Uktay Qa'an in the city of Qaraqorum with gold and silver statues made so as wine and qumiz, deposited in them, should run out of their mouths. "It is indeed the only representation of Qaraqorum at the time when it was the capital of all the Mongol dominions, to supplement the descriptions given by Juvayni and at first hand by Friar William of Rubruck." in An Unknown Fragment of the "Jāmi' al-tawārīkh" in the Asiatic Society of Bengal, Basil Gray Ars Orientalis, Vol. 1 (1954), pp. 65-75 (23 pages) https://www.jstor.org/stable/4628983 The fountain was the work of the Parisian slave Guillaume Boucher : "...the various works of western origin mentioned by William of Rubruck. He himself met the craftsman responsible for the most spectacular of these, Guillaume Boucher, a slave from the capture of Belgrade in 1242, but a skilled silversmith of Paris. His major work was the fountain, which is precisely the subject of our illustration." in An Unknown Fragment of the "Jāmi' al-tawārīkh" in the Asiatic Society of Bengal, Basil Gray Ars Orientalis, Vol. 1 (1954), pp. 65-75 (23 pages) https://www.jstor.org/stable/4628983

files.title: File:Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah confronts Chinggis Khan across the Indus. Rashid al-Din, Jami‘ al-tawarikh, National Library of Russia, St Petersburg, MS. Dorn 289, fols. 125v–126r (Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah detail).jpg
files.description: Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah confronts Chinggis Khan across the Indus. Rashid al-Din, Jami‘ al-tawarikh, National Library of Russia, St Petersburg, MS. Dorn 289, fols. 125v–126r (Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah detail)
files.credit: The Illustration of History in Persian Manuscripts Figure 3 "A later copy of the Jami‘ al-tawarikh, produced in Turusht [which was near the town of Rayy (near present-day Tehran)] in 935/1529 and now in St Petersburg from the library of the shrine at Ardabil, contains 29 paintings, including the exploit of Jalal al-Din Khwarazmshah crossing the Indus (Figure 3).57 This is a double-page painting (the only one in this manuscript), showing the sultan on the left-hand page, not looking at all like someone who has just plunged across the Indus, but standing with his beautifully caparisoned horse and wiping his sword dry with a blue cloth. It reflects the text to the extent that he still has his shield over his shoulder and has planted his banner defiantly on the bank. Perhaps more interesting is the right-hand side of the painting, which shows Chinggis Khan turning back towards his sons and entourage, remarking on Jalal al-Din’s valour." The Illustration of History in Persian Manuscripts page 10

files.title: File:Kayi Yabgu enthroned, in the council of Tuman, Köl Erki, Kayı Yavgu Han and Korkut. Jami al-Tawarikh, 1426-30 Herat, folio 387a (TSMK, H.1653).jpg
files.description: Tuman in the Jami al-Tawarikh, 1426-30 Herat, folio 387a (TSMK, H.1653) "According to Reşideddin, Dede Korkut lived in the period after Oğuz Kagan. According to the information in the work, upon the will of Oğuz Kagan, Gün Khan succeeded his father. After Gün Khan, Dip Yabgu succeeded him. He also preserved the order established by his grandfather Oğuz Kagan. After Gün Khan, his other son Kurs Yabgu succeeded him. Then, Kuru Yasak Yabgu, İnal Yabgu, İnalsır Yasak Yabgu, Ala Atlı Kış Donlu Kayı İnal Khan, Tuman Khan , Diken Bile Er Biçken Kayı Yabgu Khan ascended to the throne in order. According to the work, Korkut lived in the time of Ala Atlı Kış Donlu Kayı İnal Khan, Köl Erki Khan , Tuman Khan , Diken Bile Er Biçken Kayı Yabgu Khan . Korkut here is Dede Korkut." p.12 "Beginning with Reshid ud-din, in the early fourteenth century, historians of the Oghuz described Korkut as a competent statesman and diplomat who served several of the ninth- and tenth-century kings who made Yeni Kent their capital: Inal Sir Yabgu , Kayi Inal Khan , and Tuman (whom he also named)." The Book of Dede Korkut: A Turkish Epic

files.title: File:Messager de Djengiz Khân à Nîshâbûr.jpeg
files.description: Messengers of Genghis Khan at the gates of Nishapur. Supplément Persan 1443 f.94 "94. Genghis Khan on horseback, followed by three Mongol officers in front of the walls of the city of Nishapur; two Muslims stand on the walls; Djingiz is armed with a bow and a quiver; one of the Mongol horsemen holds a standard on which we see the current coat of arms of the Qajars, the sun rising behind a lion." Revue des bibliothèques, Volume 10, p.190 "The earliest-known representation [of the sun and lion] as a banner device ( Figure 18 ) is from a miniature painting illustrating a copy, dated 826/1423, of the Šāh-nāma of Šams-al-Dīn Kāšānī—an epic composition on the Mongol conquest (Bibliothèque Nationale, suppl. no. 1443). It shows several (Mongol?) horsemen approaching a walled city (Nīšāpūr), and one of them carries a tall banner which is crowned by a spear-head within a crescent moon (the māhča-ye lewāʾ) and its square background bears a lion passant with a rising sun on its back and two floating pennons (Blochet, 1928, III, p. 180). A similar early depiction ( Figure 19 ) is on a large, double-paged miniature dated ca. 865/1460 ( Martin, Pls. 60 f. )." Encyclopedia Iranica
files.credit: Bibliothèque nationale de France. Département des Manuscrits. Division orientale. Supplément persan 1443, fol. 94

files.title: File:Mohammed kaaba 1315 bew.jpg
files.description: Prophet Muhammad solves a dispute over lifting the black stone into position at al-Kaaba. Note from pp. 100-101 of "The illustrations to the World history of Rashid al-Din / David Talbot Rice ; edited by Basil Gray. Edinburgh : Edinburgh University Press, c1976." - In the center, Prophet Muhammad, with two long hair plaits, places the stone on a carpet held at the four corners by representatives of the four tribes, so that all have the honor of lifting it. The carpet is a kelim from Central Asia. Behind, two other men lift the black curtain which conceals the doors of the sanctuary. This work may be assigned to the Master of the Scenes from the Life of the Prophet.
files.credit: Jami' al-Tavarikh ("The Compendium of Chronicles" or "The Universal History") This illustration is in a folio in the Oriental Manuscript Section of the Edinburgh University Library, Special Collections and Archives

files.description: Miniature illustration on vellum from the book Jami’ al-Tawarikh, by Rashid al-Din, published in Tabriz, Persia, 1307 A.D. It depicts Prophet Mohammed as he solves a dispute over lifting the black stone into position at the Kaaba. The history tells how, when Mohammed was still a young man, the Kaaba was being rebuilt and a dispute arose between the various clans in Mecca over who had the right to rededicate the black stone. Mohammed resolved the argument by placing the stone on a cloth and having members of each clan lift the cloth together, raising the black stone into place cooperatively.
files.credit: Own work

files.title: File:Sham Ghazan, mausoleum of Ghazan in Tabriz (also called Gunbad-i 'Âlî) (BNF, Supplément Persan 1113 f.256v-257).jpg
files.description: Possibly similar mausoleum. p.40 Sham Ghazan (Tomb of Ghazan), Tabrîz (mosque Gunbad-i 'Âlî) (BNF, Supplément Persan 1113 f.256v-257). [1] "The Ghazaniyya, Tabriz, representation of the mausoleum (in the centre), adjacent madrasa (Islamic school, left) and khanaqah (Sufi lodge, right). Rashid al-Din. Jami‘ al-tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), dated ca. 1420–1430, MS Supplément Persan 1113, ff. 256v-257r., 320 × 230mm. Bibliothèque Nationale de France, Paris." Samarqand’s Congregational Mosque of Bibi Khanum as a Representation of Timurid Legitimacy and Rulership, October 2023, Manazir Journal 5:59-87, Elena Paskaleva This is the last miniature from the 1420-1430 Jami al-Tawarikh , in the final part where the achievements of Ghazan are listed, including the building of the Sham Ghazan (Gazaniyya): "He also ordered another city larger than the encompassment of Old Tabriz built in Shamb (also called Shamm), where the Abwabu’l birr was constructed, in such a way that it encompassed the Abwabu’l-birr and most of its gardens. He called it Ghazania, and he ordered that merchants coming from Anatolia and Europe unload there, but the customs official for there and the city of Tabriz is the same lest there be dispute." Rashiduddin Fazlullah’s Jami u't-tawarikh: Compendium of Chronicles: A History of the Mongols Part One. English Translation & Annotation p 684 (Note 1: The complex of charitable institutions founded by Ghazan Khan in Shamb, Tabriz. The name Abwabu’l-birr (‘gates of piety’) is both a generic term for such institutions and, apparently here, the specific name given to the complex. For the terms of endowment, see text pp. 997ff. below. p.668) Sometimes called "Gunbad i 'Ali": "He died on Sunday, 11 May 1304 in the thirty-third year of his life, and his body, transported amid universal mourning to Tabriz, was laid to rest in the Gunbad-i-‘Ali, the mausoleum he had himself designed and erected." (" Ali dome ") Dynastic and Political History of the Il-Khans by John Andrew Boyle, p.93

files.title: File:The Buyid al-Dawla brothers in a struggle for succession. Jami‛ al-Tawarikh University of Edinburgh Ms Or 20 f.110v (cropped).jpg
files.description: * "Detail of miniature from the Compendium of Chronicles by Rashid al-Din. Shows the forces of 'Adud and Mu'ayyid al-Dawla, two brothers of the Buyid Dynasty, which controlled most of Iran and Iraq during the 10th and 11th centuries, attacking the troops of their brother Rukn al'Dawla, in a struggle for succession. Two horsemen can be seen in combat in the centre of the picture, while other mounted troops look on from either side. A real historical event, the battle took place in September 976CE. " [1]
